rejected.title: Aboriginal medicines and research
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have used plants as medicines for thousands of years. This knowledge was built up and passed on over many generations.
Scientists may study these plants to find out which chemicals in them have an effect on the body. This research can lead to new treatments.
Consent means the knowledge holders agree, with full information, before their knowledge is used. Research done without it can take cultural knowledge without permission.
Fair sharing of benefits means the community that holds the knowledge shares in the results, such as recognition, a say in how it is used, or a share of any income.
rejected.remember: Research using Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander plant knowledge needs consent and a fair share of the benefits.

a.q: Why does research on traditional plant medicines raise a question of consent?
opts: The knowledge is held by a community, which should agree
The plants are always rare and need legal protection
Scientists cannot test plants without a community's help
Traditional knowledge is less reliable than lab results
a.why: The knowledge was built up and held by a community, so the community should agree, with full information, before it is used. Consent is about permission to use the knowledge, not about whether the plants work or can be tested.
a.clue: Think about who holds the knowledge before the scientists arrive.

b.q: A company develops a skin cream from a plant after learning of its use from a community in northern Australia. The community agreed to the research. It receives no credit and no share of the income. Which issue remains?
opts: Fair sharing of benefits
Consent to the research
Herd immunity in the community
Resistance to the cream's chemicals
b.why: The community agreed, so consent was met. The problem is that it received no recognition or share of the income, which is a question of fair sharing of benefits. Consent and fair sharing are two separate questions, so agreeing to the research does not settle the second.
b.clue: The community said yes at the start. What did it get at the end?

draft.title: Aboriginal medicines and research
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have used plants as medicines for thousands of years. This knowledge was built up and passed on over many generations.
Scientists may study these plants to find which chemicals in them affect the body. This research can lead to new treatments.
Consent
the knowledge holders agree, with full information, before their knowledge is used. Without it, research can take cultural knowledge without permission.
Fair sharing
the community that holds the knowledge shares in the results. This can mean recognition, a say in how the knowledge is used, or a share of any income.
draft.remember: Using Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander plant knowledge raises two questions: was there consent, and are the benefits shared fairly?

a.q: Which situation best shows consent in research on a traditional plant medicine?
opts: Elders are told the aims and agree before the study starts
Scientists publish their findings once the study is finished
A museum already holds a record of how the plant was used
The plant is grown in a laboratory so it can be tested
a.why: Consent means the knowledge holders agree, with full information, before the knowledge is used. Publishing results or finding an old record happens without the community's agreement, so neither is consent.
a.clue: Who must agree, and when must they agree?

b.q: A company learns of a plant's medicinal use from a community and tests its chemicals, without asking the community first. It later gives the community credit and a fair share of the income. Which question is still unresolved?
opts: Consent was not sought before the knowledge was used
The community received no share of the benefits
The community received no credit for its knowledge
The chemicals in the plant were never tested
b.why: The company never asked the community before using its knowledge, so consent is still missing. Credit and a fair share of income answer the question of sharing benefits, but they do not replace agreement given beforehand.
b.clue: Sharing the results afterwards is a different step from asking at the start.

a.best: Elders are told the aims and agree before the study starts

b.best: Consent was not sought before the knowledge was used

problems.detail: Why (a) says finding an old museum record 'happens without the community's agreement'. That overstates it, since a record may have been made with consent. The real point is that an existing record is not the knowledge holders agreeing to this study.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer that matches the card. The only issue is minor: why (a) wrongly suggests a museum record is always made without agreement, when the point is that it is not consent for this study.
